1:
The mourning draws four answers. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) notes that God blames him not for mourning but for exceeding in it, and that Samuel had shed no tears over the setting aside of his own family, yet mourns for Saul without measure — the one done by the people’s foolish discontent, the other by the righteous wrath of God; and to what purpose should he weep, when the decree has gone forth? John Gill (reformed) makes the same distinction, that he is blamed not for mourning but for mourning so long, which was in vain, the sentence being irreversible. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) says what the mourning amounted to, that he prayed for Saul’s restitution. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) hears the Divine Voice rousing him from his mourning inactivity: the instrument prepared with so much care was broken, but the work for which it was created must still be done.

What kind of king is provided, and anointed with what. Henry hears a contrast in the words, since the people provided themselves a king and he proved bad, and now God will provide himself one,. Wesley finds the phrase emphatical to the same end, Saul having been the product of their sinful desires while this is a king of God’s own providing, to serve his glory; and he notes that the oil here designates rather than inaugurates, since David was not made king by it but still remained a subject, the anticipation serving the comfort of good men and the assurance of David’s title. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) explains the vessel, that horns were the ancient drinking vessels of all nations, carried by travellers to take up water from the fountains. Ellicott reads the Hebrew as the oil, probably that consecrated oil kept in the tabernacle at Nob; Henry contrasts Saul’s glass vial, scanty and brittle, with David’s plentiful and durable horn.

Samuel’s fear is diagnosed, and the cover he is given defended. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) hold that such fear in a prophet not generally hesitating or timid can only be explained on the supposition that Saul was already given up to the power of the evil spirit, so that the very worst might be dreaded from his madness; and they find the anxiety well founded, since the Lord did not blame him for it but pointed out a way. Ellicott agrees the malady had made rapid progress, the king being changed from the Saul who in his very rebellion was careful to pay honour to Samuel. Henry and Gill both call it weakness of faith, Gill adding fear of man and distrust of divine power, Henry that the best men are not perfect in their faith. Clarke defends the errand: it was strictly true, and though no man should tell a lie, he is not obliged to tell the whole truth, provided he so tell it that the hearer shall not believe a lie by it.

Why Bethlehem trembled, and what sanctifying meant. Ellicott pictures the aged seer arriving with the heifer and the long horn of holy oil, so that the villagers wondered whether their remote township had been the scene of some unknown and grave crime. Keil and Delitzsch infer from the inquiry that Samuel was frequently in the habit of coming unexpectedly to one place and another to reprove and punish wrong-doing, and put the singular verb down to one elder speaking for the rest. Henry allows two fears, of God’s displeasure for the iniquities of the place, since guilt causes fear, or of Saul’s for entertaining him. Wesley glosses their question as the Hebrew for is all well? Clarke spells out the preparation: change your clothes, wash your bodies in pure water, and prepare your minds by meditation, reflection and prayer, that being in the spirit of sacrifice ye may offer acceptably.
6:
Samuel’s first guess is excused and then explained. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) finds something in the tall and stately presence of the eldest born that reminded the old man of the splendid youth of Saul, so that Eliab seemed in all respects a fit successor to the warrior the Lord had rejected; but the Divine voice gave no reply to the prophet’s mute questioning. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) grants that the prophets themselves, even when they spoke under divine direction, were as liable to mistake as other men; yet he thinks it strange that Samuel, who had been so wretchedly disappointed in Saul, whose countenance and stature had recommended him, should be so forward to judge by that rule. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) puts it down to haste, prophets sometimes speaking their own thoughts before they had consulted God. John Gill (reformed) describes the correction as a secret impulse upon his mind, as if God had spoken with an articulate voice.

The rule that replaces the eye is stated three ways. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) note that the Hebrew has man looking at the eyes, the eyes being figuratively employed, as contrasted with the heart, to denote the outward form. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) thinks it well that man should look there and confine his looks to that, for when he pretends to sound the heart he usurps the prerogative of God; and he marvels at the channel, direct inspiration arguing a holy familiarity in which Moses himself, he believes, was not more highly favoured than Samuel. Henry draws the contrast out: when God would please the people with a king he chose a comely man, but one after his own heart was not to be chosen by the outside; and he turns the passing-by of the seven into a point about sovereignty, since men dispose of honours and estates according to seniority of birth, but the elder shall serve the younger.

How many sons there were, and why one was missing, is worked out. Ellicott counts these seven with David as eight, and notes that the genealogy in Chronicles records only seven, so that one of that bright band of youths apparently died young. Gill reaches the same total from the other side, four brought up to join the three already named, of whom one we nowhere read of, perhaps dying soon after or born of another woman. Wesley allows either, a concubine’s son or an early death. Clarke infers the scene was private, Samuel and Jesse and his children being in a separate apartment before the public feast. Ellicott finds the reason for David’s absence uncertain, his beauty being of a very different type from his brothers’, probably little of stature with reddish-brown hair and a fair complexion, so that Jesse thought him of too little account to present.

What the anointing conveyed, and how much of it was understood, divides them. Henry takes no notice of the clothing, which was mean and coarse as shepherds’ coats commonly are, since David did not change his as Joseph did, and finds the look not stately like Saul’s but sweet and lovely, perhaps made handsomer by a modest blush. Clarke reads ruddy as red-haired, golden locks, hair ever associated with a delicate skin and florid complexion; Keil and Delitzsch agree it denotes the reddish hair that counted a mark of beauty in southern lands where hair is generally black, and add that corporeal beauty was one of the outward distinctions of a king. Ellicott supposes Samuel kept silence for the present and anointed him merely as an assistant in the sacrifice, adopting him as a pupil in his prophetic school. Wesley agrees the brethren were told only of some great service, so that Jesse and David alone understood the business, while the brethren could still attest the act.
14:
What departed, and what came in its place. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) sees Saul made a terror to himself, God in a way of righteous judgment withdrawing those assistances of the good Spirit by which he had been directed, animated and encouraged, so that he lost all his good qualities; for when men quench the Spirit by wilful sin he departs, and those who drive him away become of course the prey of the evil one. The trouble came by means of the corrupt humours of his body and the passions of his mind, leaving him fretful, peevish, timorous and suspicious, ever and anon starting and trembling, unfit for business and a burden to all about him. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) puts it epigrammatically, that God seems to have taken what gifts Saul had and given them to David, for what God fills not, the devil will. John Gill (reformed) itemises the loss from the Targum: the spirit of prophecy, of wisdom and prudence in civil government, and of fortitude and courage.

What the malady was, and who proposed the cure. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) describes an apparently incurable melancholy which at times blazed forth in fits of uncontrollable jealous anger, a species of insanity fatal alike to the victim and to his kingdom; and he finds Saul’s nervous, excitable temperament peculiarly subject to such influences, as earlier incidents with the prophetic schools had shown. Clarke leaves open whether this was a diabolic possession or a mere mental malady, the learned not being agreed and the case seeming to partake of both, since Satan delights to fish in troubled waters. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) report the courtiers’ advice to have the spirit charmed away by instrumental music, noting that the wise men of ancient Greece having recommended music to soothe the passions, heal mental diseases, and even check tumults among the people. Gill allows the counsellors may have been physicians called in rather than courtiers.

Whether music could touch a spirit at all is argued. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) denies it can work on the spirit directly, but reasons that the devil had no possession of Saul and only made use of the passions of his mind and the humours of his body, which music has a mighty power to qualify and sweeten; and since music prepared the Lord’s prophets to receive the good Spirit, why should it not dispose Saul to resist the evil one? Clarke reaches the same end by physiology, adopting Scheuchzer’s theory that health lies in a moderate tension of the fibres and disease in tensions morbidly weak or strong, so that the undulations which carry sound through the most solid bodies might relax the over-strained fibres and restore a free circulation. Henry grants the servants honesty in naming the distemper but wishes they had advised repentance and sent for Samuel, since their project was to make him merry and so cure him.

Who spoke for David, and how much he claimed. Keil and Delitzsch identify the speaker as one of the youths, a lower class of court servant, and hold that calling David a mighty man and a man of war presupposes no campaign, being explicable from his own later account of the lion and the bear. Ellicott notes that the word is not the one rendered servants just before, this one stressing youth, so that the speaker was probably a contemporary trained with David in Samuel’s school; he adds that David may also have helped repel the Philistine raids to which Bethlehem lay open. Gill reports and rejects the Jewish identification of the speaker as Doeg the Edomite, speaking from envy, preferring a friend who wished to promote him. Clarke records Warburton’s view that the whole passage is anticipated, the harp-playing belonging after the combat with the giant.
19:
The summons and the present are read for what they reveal. John Gill (reformed) notices that Saul sent messengers to Jesse rather than simply taking the boy, not choosing to have him without his father’s leave, though Samuel had warned that kings would do so. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) explains the gift by custom, since it was ever usual in the East to acknowledge subjection with a present, so that Jesse, the sheik of Bethlehem, would be expected to send some token of homage with his son to court. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reckons it probably the best he had. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) draw the same inference from the modesty of the items, that the customs of Israel and of Saul’s court were still simple at that time; and they reject the Greek reading of a measure of loaves for an ass laden with bread, bread not being measured in bushels.

What favour David found, and how long it held. Keil and Delitzsch take standing before him to mean serving him by playing on the harp, after which Saul took a great liking to him and named him his armour-bearer, in effect his adjutant, as a proof of satisfaction; so David came to the court as Saul’s benefactor, without the king having any suspicion of his divine election. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) adds that Saul loved him greatly and, contrary to the manner of the king, asked his father’s leave to keep him in his service. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) finds in that affection a scrap of evidence that there was something good in Saul still, who had not lost all though he had lost the kingdom; yet he doubts the office was ever exercised, David seeming to have gone back to his father for some considerable time. Ellicott agrees it was brief, supposing he returned to Samuel, who was watching over him with a view to his lofty destiny.

What spirit it was is contested from the manuscripts. Clarke observes that the word evil is absent from the common Hebrew text but present in the Vulgate, Septuagint, Targum, Syriac and Arabic and in eight of the manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi, while the Greek drops the words of God altogether and the Arabic reads by the permission of God; and the Targum’s rendering, that the spirit went up from off him, treats the malady as more than a natural disease. His own verdict is a malady of mixed kind, with too much apparent nature in it to call it all spiritual and too much supernatural influence to call it all natural. Gill reports from the same absence that Abarbinel took this to be the Spirit of God, stirring up thoughts of divine things and putting Saul in mind of his rejection, which filled him with grief.

Why the playing worked, without crediting it too much. Henry judges that it did not charm the evil spirit but made Saul’s spirit sedate, allaying those tumults of the animal spirits by which the devil had advantage against him; and he borrows a comparison, that sunbeams cannot be cut with a sword, quenched with water or blown out with wind, yet by closing the shutters may be kept out of the chamber, so music cannot work upon the devil but may shut up the passages by which he reaches the mind. He notes too that only the instrumental music is mentioned, though by the account Josephus gives David sang hymns to his harp; and Saul later found, even after conceiving an enmity to him, that no one else could do him the same service. Ellicott gathers witnesses elsewhere, Luther calling music one of the fairest gifts of God, to which Satan is a bitter enemy, and Basil making psalmody the calm of the soul, which silences the wave and repels demons.
